source.id: TITLE:Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
source.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
source.authors: Trenton Bricken; Adly Templeton; Joshua Batson; Brian Chen; Adam Jermyn; Tom Conerly; Nicholas L Turner; Cem Anil; Carson Denison; Amanda Askell; Robert Lasenby; Yifan Wu; Shauna Kravec; Nicholas Schiefer; Tim Maxwell; Nicholas Joseph; Alex Tamkin; Karina Nguyen; Brayden McLean; Josiah E Burke; Tristan Hume; Shan Carter; Tom Henighan; Chris Olah

record.file_problem: The text is long (2317 lines). I read lines 1-825 in full, plus lines 940-1170, 1360-1420 and 2085-2104. I skipped the middle global-analysis and automated-interpretability sections, the rest of the universality section, the finite-state-automata section and the appendix. A search for "split" shows that all feature-splitting material is in the parts I read. Figures and the UMAP are not in the text.
record.tranche_reason: This is the original source of the claim. It reports feature splitting across SAE sizes on a one-layer transformer. It is tagged T1 as the original measurement.
record.gate_note: Excluded as non-rows: the universality correlations between models A and B (median 0.72 for features vs 0.46 for neurons), which do not concern splitting, and the interpretability scores. The local-vs-compositional code discussion is argument with no result, so it has no row.
record.test_reason: This is the original source of V1. It trains a sequence of L1 sparse autoencoders (A/0 to A/5, fixed L1 coefficient, 512 up to 131,072 features) on the 512-neuron MLP of a one-layer transformer and follows features across sizes. The results are: base64-specific features go from 1 to 3 to many; A/0/45 splits into three A/1 features that jointly cover it; a UMAP of decoder directions shows tight same-context clusters; and a math/physics family is traced by masked activation cosine. All of this is qualitative. Besides V1, these results bear on V3: families are geometrically close, but features split and merge, so the structure is not a tree. V3 is not listed as originating here, so it gets verdicts. V1 does not.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase needs correcting. Splitting is presented as an observation, not a conjecture. As SAE width grows from 512 to 131,072, one coarse feature is replaced by several finer, still-interpretable features. For example, A/0/45 (base64) becomes three A/1 features that jointly cover it, and similar features have close dictionary directions. The refinement is not a tree, since features can both split and merge. The conjecture is a separate claim: an idealized feature set exists, and a finite dictionary returns features that cover the same territory at coarser resolution and lower specificity. From this the authors infer that the 'correct number of features' matters less than it seems and that small dictionaries can act as summaries. They attribute the clustering to correlated features with similar output actions, which their toy-model theory of superposition missed.
record.recipe_differences: Original source. L1 sparse autoencoder on MLP activations of a one-layer transformer, with dictionaries from 512 to 131,072 features. The analysis is qualitative, using UMAP, masked cosine similarity and manual inspection.
record.method_sensitivity: The links between coarse and fine features use a masked cosine similarity with a threshold of about 0.4. The authors chose that threshold to keep the graph readable (footnote 32). The P features were found manually. The authors raise the possibility that the local code of token-in-context features is a quirk of the L1 penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: Split siblings differ in their downstream logit effects, not only in when they fire. The base64 digit feature A/1/2364 down-weights digits, which the authors trace to BPE tokenization. Finer math features (A/2/15021, A/2/4878, A/2/2609) make more topic-specific predictions than A/0/341. The authors note that logit effects are not an input to dictionary learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features produced by splitting carry distinct downstream effects in the model, not only distinct activation patterns.

record.problems: Splitting is shown by a few case studies and by UMAP and cosine graphs, with no quantitative coverage or partition measure. There is one small model, no error bars, and no controls. The authors present the idealized-features picture as a conjecture.
record.rows_left_out: I did not read the unread middle sections or the appendix, which may hold more splitting detail. Nothing else was left out.

untested.parts: No verdict, since this is V1's original source. Even here, coverage and direction similarity are shown only qualitatively, with no coverage fraction or cosine values.
The whole version. Only one-layer transformers were studied (A, and B as a second seed), and splitting was analysed only on A. No large model or open SAE release was used.

Whether families mirror a hierarchy of concepts in the model's own representation, beyond activation-overlap links and the greater logit specificity of finer features. There is no quantitative test of nesting or geometry.

The whole version. No parent/child latent pairs are identified or scored for absorption, no absorption rate is given, and size or sparsity is not varied to see whether gaps persist. An absorption-like sensitivity gap is noted only anecdotally (see missing).

No SAE stitching or meta-SAE decomposition. Novel latents are not separated from reconstructed ones, and atomicity is not tested. The only related results are that more and rarer features keep appearing up to 131,072 features, and the split-and-merge observation (see missing).

No alternative training objective is tested. Whether token-in-context features (which arise by splitting) are a quirk of the L1 penalty or a genuine local code is argued, not tested. The authors lean toward a genuine local code 'to some extent'.

missing.what: The three A/1 base64 split features have similar decoder (dictionary) vectors, but their encoder vectors are tilted apart to tell them apart. The Discussion adds that the digit and letter base64 features share predictions and have geometrically close directions. This is direct, feature-level evidence that children lie near each other and near the parent's direction.
missing.locator: Appendix, Autoencoder Architecture, 'Decoder Weights Not Tied'; Discussion, Theories of Superposition

missing.what: Sensitivity gaps in a main context feature are 'often explained by the activity of another' feature. The Arabic feature A/1/3450 does not fire on the 'al-' prefix where another Arabic-script feature, A/1/3134, does. Similar gaps occur for base64 digits (A/1/2364) and Hebrew \xd7 (A/1/1016). This is coverage by sibling features (V1). It is also an absorption-like gap, but the text does not establish that the gap-filling features are children of the main feature, and it does not vary size or sparsity.
missing.locator: Detailed Investigations, Arabic Script Feature, Activation Sensitivity; Base64 Feature; Hebrew Feature

missing.what: As dictionary size grows to 131,072, more and rarer features keep appearing, which the authors read as 'we have not exhausted the features'. The Summary says new features keep being found as the SAE scales. The Discussion says the 'correct number of features' may not be well-posed, while the conjecture of an idealized feature set says otherwise. This bears on whether any size gives a complete set. Together with R4's split-and-merge result, it is the study's only evidence relevant to V5.
missing.locator: Appendix, Feature Density Histograms; Summary of Results; Discussion, Theories of Superposition

record.verdict_notes: I read the whole text, lines 1-2309; everything after the footnotes is references. Figures, including the UMAP, the coverage plot and the split/merge graph, are not in the text. The record says read_status 'full', but its file_problem field says the reader skipped sections. I read those sections. They add the missing items above but no new splitting experiments. No V1 label is given because this study is V1's original source. The V3 labels are given only because config.json lists ['V1'] as this original's scope. If Iris treats Bricken et al. as the origin of the 'feature families' idea (V3), drop those labels. All evidence is qualitative: case studies, a UMAP, and an activation-similarity graph with a threshold chosen for readability. There is one small model, with no error bars and no controls for splitting. The text contains no instructions aimed at the reader.

versions.untested_parts: Only qualitative case studies. There is no quantitative coverage measure for the splits.
Only a one-layer transformer was studied.
Geometry is shown by UMAP and masked cosine similarity of activations. There is no explicit hierarchy test.
The authors discuss whether a local code is an artifact of the L1 penalty but report no experiment.

rows.check: The measure is masked cosine similarity of feature activations, not decoder geometry. It links features above a threshold of about 0.4, which was chosen to keep the graph readable (footnote 32). The intermediate runs are not named in the text, and the figure is missing. 'Partial' reflects the authors' statement that features both split and merge, so refinement is not a clean replacement or tree. Finer features do have more specific logit predictions (A/0/341 vs A/2/15021, A/2/4878, A/2/2609).

The encoder-tilt note (A/1 base64 features: similar dictionary vectors, encoder vectors 'more tilted away') is in the appendix section 'Decoder Weights Not Tied', lines 1811-1813. statements.correction: SAEs A/0 to A/5 have a fixed L1 coefficient and run from 512 (1x) to 131,072 (256x) features (lines 57, 443, 886). The summary says features split as width grows from 512 to over 131,000 (line 131). The splitting examples (base64, UMAP, math/physics) use A/0 to A/2. A/4 has over a hundred 'the' features, often connected by splitting (lines 964-966).
statements.problem: Gives the study's setting as dictionary sizes 512 (A/0) to 16,384 (A/2). The study trains A/0 to A/5 up to 131,072 and states splitting across that whole range.
